blocks.text: Scene: The hall of David Bliss’s house is very comfortable and extremely untidy. There are several of Simon’s cartoons scattered about the walls, masses of highly coloured American and classical music strewn about the piano, and lots of flowers and comfortable furniture. A staircase ascends to a small balcony leading to the bedrooms, David’s study and Simon’s room. There is a door leading to the library down R. A service door above it under the stairs. There are French windows at back, and the front door on the L.
When the curtain rises it is about three o’clock on a Saturday afternoon in June.
Simon, in an extremely dirty tennis shirt and baggy grey flannel trousers, is crouched in the middle of the floor, cutting out squares from cartridge paper.
Sorel, more neatly dressed, is stretched on the sofa, reading a very violently bound volume of poems which have been sent to her by an aspiring friend.
I wish she hadn’t sent me the beastly book. I must say something nice about it.
She used to be such fun before she married that gloomy little man.
I know I didn’t, but I’m going to in a minute, when I’ve finished this.
I sometimes wish we were more normal and bouncing, Simon.
I should like to be a fresh, open-air girl with a passion for games.
She’s learning the names of the flowers by heart.
I always distrust her when she becomes the Squire’s lady.
She’s been at it hard all day﻿—she tapped the barometer this morning.
She’s probably got a plan about impressing somebody.
Some dreary, infatuated young man will appear soon, I expect.
Not today? You don’t think she’s asked anyone down today, do you?
I don’t know. Has Father noticed anything?
No; he’s too immersed in work.
I didn’t think you’d care one way or another.
How exciting! I’ve never heard of him.
I shouldn’t flaunt your ignorance if I were you﻿—it makes you look silly.
He rolls up the cartridge paper.
He’s a frightfully well-known diplomatist﻿—I met him at the Mainwarings’ dance.
He’ll need all his diplomacy here.
I warned him not to expect good manners, but I hope you’ll be as pleasant to him as you can.
You could be a little more polished without losing caste.
Will he have the papers with him?
I wish you’d confine your biting irony to your caricatures, Simon.
And I wish you’d confine your girlish infatuations to London, and not force them on your defenceless family.
I shall keep him out of your way as much as possible.
Clara, has Mother asked anyone down this weekend?
I don’t know, dear. There isn’t much food in the house, and Amy’s got toothache.
I’ve got some oil of cloves somewhere.
She tried that, but it only burnt her tongue. The poor girl’s been writhing about in the scullery like one o’clock.
You haven’t forgotten to put those flowers in the Japanese room?
The Japanese room is essentially feminine, and entirely unsuited to the Pet of the Foreign Office.
The room looks lovely, dear﻿—you needn’t worry. Just like your mother’s dressing-room on a first night.
I think Sorel’s beginning to be ashamed of us all, Clara﻿—I don’t altogether blame her; we are very slapdash.
Are you going to leave that picture in the guests’ bathroom, dear? I don’t know if it’s quite the thing﻿—lots of pink, naked women rolling about in a field.
Clara’s looking tired. We ought to have more servants and not depend on her so much.
You know we can never keep them. You’re right about us being slapdash, Simon. I wish we weren’t.
It must, I think﻿—to other people.
It’s not our fault﻿—it’s the way we’ve been brought up.
Well, if we’re clever enough to realise that, we ought to be clever enough to change ourselves.
I’m not sure that I want to.
The people we like put up with it because they like us.
What do you mean, exactly, by bad manners? Lack of social tricks and small-talk?
We never attempt to look after people when they come here.
Why should we? It’s loathsome being looked after.
Yes, but people like little attentions. We’ve never once asked anyone if they’ve slept well.
I consider that an impertinence, anyhow.
I’m going to try to improve.
You’re only going on like this because you’ve got a mania for a diplomatist. You’ll soon return to normal.
It’s no use worrying, darling; we see things differently, I suppose, and if people don’t like it they must lump it.
Life must be terribly dull for her now, with nothing to do.
She’ll go back soon, I expect; people never retire from the stage for long.
Father will be livid if she does.
You look awfully dirty, Simon. What have you been doing?
She proceeds to take off her goloshes.
Poor dear! There’s some oil of cloves in my medicine cupboard. Who is Amy?
How extraordinary! She doesn’t look Amy a bit, does she? Much more Flossie.﻿—Give me a cigarette.
Delphiniums are those stubby red flowers, aren’t they?
No, darling, they’re tall and blue.
Yes, of course. The red ones are somebody’s name﻿—asters, that’s it. I knew it was something opulent. I do hope Clara has remembered about the Japanese room.
Yes; I told her to put some flowers in it and take Simon’s flannels out of the wardrobe drawer.
Mind! How dared you do such a thing?
That makes it much worse. We must wire and put him off at once.
Well, we’ll tell Clara to say we’ve been called away.
You mean to stand there in cold blood and tell me you’ve asked a complete stranger down for the weekend, and that you want to see him!
I fail to see how that helps matters. Where’s he going to sleep?
Oh, no, he isn’t﻿—Sandy Tyrell is sleeping in it.
There now! What did I tell you?
Why didn’t you tell us, Mother?
I did. I’ve talked of nothing but Sandy Tyrell for days. I adore Sandy Tyrell.
He’s a perfect darling, and madly in love with me﻿—at least, it isn’t me really, it’s my Celebrated Actress glamour﻿—but it gives me a divinely cosy feeling. I met him at Nora Trent’s.
Mother, I wish you’d give up this sort of thing.
What exactly do you mean by “this sort of thing,” Sorel?
You know perfectly well what I mean.
Are you attempting to criticise me?
I should have thought you’d be above encouraging silly callow young men who are infatuated by your name.
That may be true, but I shall allow nobody but myself to say it. I hoped you’d grow up a good daughter to me, not a critical aunt.
Cheap! Nonsense! What about your diplomatist?
Surely that’s a little different, dear?
If you mean that because you happen to be a vigorous ingénue of nineteen you have the complete monopoly of any amorous adventure there may be about, I feel it my firm duty to disillusion you.
Anyone would think I was eighty, the way you go on. It was a great mistake not sending you to boarding schools, and you coming back and me being your elder sister.
It wouldn’t have been any use. Everyone knows we’re your son and daughter.
Only because I was stupid enough to dandle you about in front of cameras when you were little. I knew I should regret it.
I don’t see any point in trying to be younger than you are.
At your age, dear, it would be indecent if you did.
But, Mother darling, don’t you see, it’s awfully undignified for you to go flaunting about with young men?
I don’t flaunt about﻿—I never have. I’ve been morally an extremely nice woman all my life﻿—more or less﻿—and if dabbling gives me pleasure, I don’t see why I shouldn’t dabble.
But it oughtn’t to give you pleasure any more.
You know, Sorel, you grow more damnably feminine every day. I wish I’d brought you up differently.
You will be nice to Sandy, won’t you?
My dear, he’s frightfully athletic, and all those hot-water pipes will sap his vitality.
He won’t notice them; he’s probably used to scorching tropical Embassies with punkahs waving and everything.
He’s sure to be deadly, anyhow.
You’re getting far too blasé and exclusive, Simon.
Nothing of the sort. Only I loathe being hearty with your men friends.
You’ve never been even civil to any of my friends, men or women.
Anyhow, the Japanese room’s a woman’s room, and a woman ought to have it.
I promised it to Sandy﻿—he loves anything Japanese.
Myra Arundel. I’ve asked her down.
I’ve asked Myra down for the weekend﻿—she’s awfully amusing.
Well, all I can say is, it’s beastly of you. You might have warned me. What on earth will Richard say?
This is too much! Do you mean to tell me, Simon﻿—
Myra Arundel is straining freedom to its utmost limits.
No, dear, I detest her. She’s far too old for you, and she goes about using Sex as a sort of shrimping net.
It’s no use being cross. You know perfectly well I dislike her, and that’s why you never told me she was coming until too late to stop her. It’s intolerable of you.
You’re afraid he’ll like her too much.
That was an offensive remark, Simon, and rather silly.
She’s not a vampire, and I never said I was in love with her.
He’s crazy about her. She butters him up and admires his sketches.
What about you picking up old gentlemen at dances?

You’ve both upset me thoroughly. I wanted a nice, restful weekend, with moments of Sandy’s ingenuous affection to warm the cockles of my heart when I felt in the mood, and now the house is going to be full of discord﻿—not enough food, everyone fighting for the bath﻿—perfect agony! I wish I were dead!
You needn’t worry about Myra and me. We shall keep out of everyone’s way.
I shall take Richard on the river all day tomorrow.
I absolutely forbid you to go near the punt.
I see no reason for there to be any noise, unless Sandy What’s-his-name is given to shouting.
If you’re rude to Sandy I shall be extremely angry.
He’s coming all the way down specially to be nice to me﻿—
Why are you all making such a noise?
Why hasn’t Clara brought me my tea?
Do stop firing questions at me, David.
Why are you all so irritable? What’s happened?
Here’s your tea. I’m sorry I’m late with it. Amy forgot to put the kettle on﻿—she’s got terrible toothache.
Poor girl! Give her some oil of cloves.
If anyone else mentions oil of cloves, I shall do something desperate.
She was in the garden this morning.
I suppose no one thought of giving her any lunch?
I put it down by the kitchen table as usual, but she never came in for it.
She isn’t old enough yet. She might have fallen into the river, for all you care. I think it’s a shame!
Don’t you worry your head﻿—Zoe won’t come to any harm; she’s too wily.
He takes his tray and goes upstairs; then he turns.
He goes off, leaving behind him a deathly silence.
I should like someone to play something very beautiful to me on the piano.
What does Father mean by going on like that?
In view of the imminent reception, you’d better go and shave, Simon.
This is going to be the blackest Saturday till Monday we’ve ever spent.
Don’t sympathise with me; it’s only temper.
Richard’ll have to have “Little Hell” and that horrible flapper the Japanese room.
Drawing him forcibly into her arms so that there is a charming little motherly picture.
Now then, Mother, none of that!
You were being beautiful and sad.
But I am beautiful and sad.
You’re not particularly beautiful, darling, and you never were.
Glancing at herself in the glass.
Well, please don’t say it again, because it annoys me.
Give me another of those disgusting cigarettes﻿—I don’t know where they came from.
I’m going to forget entirely about all these dreadful people arriving. My mind henceforward shall be a blank on the subject.
It’s all very fine, Mother, but﻿—
I made a great decision this morning.
Aren’t you going to tell us?
Of course. I meant it was a secret from your father.
I’m going back to the stage.
I’m stagnating, you see. I won’t stagnate as long as there’s breath left in my body.
Do you think it’s wise? You retired so very finally last year. What excuse will you give for returning so soon?
My public, dear﻿—letters from my public!
One or two. That’s what decided me, really﻿—I ought to have had hundreds.
We’ll write some lovely ones, and you can publish them in the papers.
You will be dignified about it all, won’t you, darling?
Oh, it’s appalling﻿—but I love it. It makes me laugh.
From the moment Victor comes in it’s strong﻿—tremendously strong.﻿ ﻿… Be Victor a minute, Sorel﻿—
Do you mean when he comes in at the end of the act?
Yes, you know﻿—“Is this a game?”
“So many illusions shattered﻿—so many dreams trodden in the dust!”
I’m George now﻿—“I don’t understand! You and Victor﻿—My God!”

“I’ve given you all that makes life worth living﻿—my youth, my womanhood, and now my child. Would you tear the very heart out of me? I tell you that it’s infamous that men like you should be allowed to pollute society. You have ruined my life﻿—I have nothing left﻿—nothing. God in heaven, where am I to turn for help.﻿ ﻿…”
Clara﻿—before you open the door﻿—we shall be eight for dinner.
And for breakfast, lunch, tea, and dinner tomorrow.
I shall have to﻿—they can’t sleep in the passage.
It can’t be helped﻿—nothing can be helped. It’s fate﻿—everything that happens is fate. That’s always a great comfort to me.
Pert I may be, but I ’ave got some thought for others. Eight for dinner﻿—Amy going home early. It’s more nor less than an imposition.
Hadn’t you better let them all in?
I mean, you didn’t meet anyone at the station?
I motored down; my car’s outside. Would you like me to meet anybody?
Oh, no. I must introduce you. This is my daughter Sorel, and my son Simon.
You must forgive me for having rather peculiar children. Have you got a bag or anything?
We’d better leave it there for the moment, as Clara has to get the tea. We’ll find you a room afterwards.
I’ve been looking forward to this most awfully.
It is nice, isn’t it? You can see as far as Marlow on a clear day, they tell me.
I meant I’ve been looking forward to seeing you.
How perfectly sweet of you. Would you like a drink?
Sitting on sofa and motioning him to sit beside her.
I’m boxing again in a couple of weeks.
I must come to your first night.
I’m so glad. You know, you mustn’t mind if Simon and Sorel insult you a little﻿—they’ve been very bad-tempered lately.
It’s awfully funny you having a grown-up son and daughter at all. I can hardly believe it.
I don’t wonder. You know, it’s frightfully queer the way I’ve been planning to know you for ages, and I never did until last week.
I liked you from the first, really, because you’re such a nice shape.
Small hips and lovely long legs﻿—I wish Simon had smaller hips. Do you think you could teach him to box?
That’s just the trouble﻿—I’m afraid he won’t like. He’s so dreadfully un﻿—that sort of thing. But never mind; you must use your influence subtly. I’m sure David would be pleased.
Why do you say “Oh” like that? Didn’t you know I had a husband?
No, he’s not dead; he’s upstairs.
You’re quite different from what you were the other day.
I love my garden, you know﻿—it’s so peaceful and quaint. I spend long days dreaming away in it﻿—you know how one dreams.
Have you ever seen me on the stage?
That thing when you pretended to cheat at cards to save your husband’s good name.
You were absolutely wonderful. That was when I first fell in love with you.
Yes; you were so frightfully pathetic and brave.
I feel such a fool, telling you what I think, as though it mattered.
Of course it matters﻿—to me, anyhow.
It seems too good to be true﻿—sitting here and talking as though we were old friends.
Do I? Give me a cigarette and let’s put our feet up.
They settle themselves comfortably at opposite ends of the sofa, smoking.
You must teach Simon﻿—he always gets the pole stuck.
You’re so gallant and chivalrous﻿—much more like an American than an Englishman.
I should like to go on saying nice things to you forever.
Is anyone else coming to stay?
Anyone else! You don’t know﻿—you just don’t know. Give me my hat.
I was wrong. It’s going to be very noisy, with herds of angry people stamping about.
Did you come by the four-thirty?
Didn’t you see anyone at the station?
Yes; several people, but I didn’t know they were coming here.
Sorel said it was going to be just ourselves this weekend.
Yes﻿—didn’t she tell you she’d asked me? Weren’t you expecting me?
Simon muttered something about your coming, but Sorel didn’t mention it. Wasn’t that odd of her?
I never knew you were coming until a little while ago.
It’s heavenly here﻿—after London. The heat was terrible when I left. You look awfully well, Judith. Rusticating obviously agrees with you.
I’m glad you think so. Personally, I feel that a nervous breakdown is imminent.
My dear, how ghastly! What’s the matter?
Nothing’s the matter yet, Myra, but I have presentiments. Come upstairs, Sandy, and I’ll show you your room.
I’ll send Simon down to you. He’s shaving, I think, but you won’t mind that, will you?
She goes off. Myra makes a slight grimace after her, then she helps herself to a cigarette and wanders about the hall﻿—she might almost play the piano a little; anyhow, she is perfectly at home.
Simon comes downstairs very fast, putting on his coat. He has apparently finished his toilet.
I’m more than cool really, but it’s not climatic coolness. I’ve been mentally chilled to the marrow by Judith’s attitude.
Nothing very much. She was bouncing about on the sofa with a hearty young thing in flannels, and seemed to resent my appearance rather.
You mustn’t take any notice of Mother.
I’ll try not to, but it’s difficult.
She’s annoyed today because Father and Sorel have been asking people down without telling her.
Poor dear! I quite see why.
Are you pleased to see me?
Of course. That’s why I came.
I feel most colossally temperamental﻿—I should like to kiss you and kiss you and kiss you and break everything in the house and then jump into the river.
You’re everything I want you to be﻿—absolutely everything. Marvellous clothes, marvellous looks, marvellous brain﻿—Oh, God, it’s terrible.﻿ ﻿…
I dined with Charlie Templeton last night.

Well, you’re a devil. You only did it to annoy me. He’s far too plump, and he can’t do anything but dither about the Embassy in badly-cut trousers. You loathe him really; you know you do﻿—you’re too intelligent not to. You couldn’t like him and me at the same time﻿—it’s impossible!
But you’re callous﻿—that’s what it is, callous! You don’t care a damn. You don’t love me a bit, do you?
Love’s a very big word, Simon.
It isn’t﻿—it’s tiny. What are we to do?
We can’t go on like this.
I’m not going on like anything.
Yes, you are; you’re going on like Medusa, and there are awful snakes popping their heads out at me from under your hat﻿—I shall be turned to stone in a minute, and then you’ll be sorry.
Tell me what you’ve been doing﻿—everything.
What did you do after you’d dined with Charlie Templeton?
Well, I don’t mind a bit. I hope you ate a lot and enjoyed yourself﻿—there!
Generous boy! Come and kiss me.
You’re only playing up to me now; you don’t really want to a bit.
This weekend’s going to be strenuous.
Hell upon earth﻿—fifteen million people in the house. We’ll get up at seven and rush away down the river.
Don’t let either of us agree to anything we say﻿—we’ll both be difficult. I love being difficult.
But I’m in the most lovely mood now. Just seeing you makes me feel grand﻿—
Yes; he’s working on a new novel.
Doesn’t he? He drinks too much tea, though.
It can’t do him much harm, surely?
Oh, that poor thing with hot hands! We’ll ignore him.
I thought he looked rather nice.
You must be mad. He looked disgusting.
Catching her hand and kissing it.
He pulls her down and kisses her.
She goes upstairs, humming a tune.
Hallo. Did you have a nice journey?
Yes, thank you, very nice. I met Miss Coryton at the station. We introduced ourselves while we were waiting for the only taxi to come back.
No; I mean I recognised you as the one who took the taxi.
Yes; she’ll be down in a minute. Come out into the garden, Myra﻿—
Grabbing her hand and dragging her off.
Have you ever met him before?
I wonder if he knows you’re here.
Perhaps that funny woman who opened the door will tell him.
It was fortunate that we met at the station.
I’m frightfully glad. I should have been terrified arriving all by myself.
I do hope the weather will keep good over Sunday﻿—the country round here is delightful.
There’s nowhere like England in the spring and summer.
Yes, I’ve always heard Spain was awfully nice.
Except for the bullfights. No one who ever really loved horses could enjoy a bullfight.
Nor anyone who loved bulls either.
I’ve always wanted to go to Italy.
Yes, I’ve always heard Rome was lovely.
Have you ever been abroad at all?
Oh, yes; I went to Dieppe once﻿—we had a house there for the summer.
Russia used to be a wonderful country before the war.
It must have been.﻿ ﻿… Was that her?
You mustn’t worry. They’re a very Bohemian family, I believe.
Couldn’t we ring a bell, or anything?
He finds bell and presses it.
It’s always a little embarrassing coming to a strange house for the first time. You’ll like Sorel﻿—she’s charming.
Do you mind if I smoke?
Oh, Richard, I’m dreadfully sorry. I didn’t know you were here.
We’ve been here a good while.
How awful! Please forgive me. I was upstairs.
Have you come to see Father?
He’s in his study﻿—you’d better go up.
She takes her to the top of the stairs.
I hope Father will find her a comfort.
Tell me one thing, Sorel, did your father and mother know I was coming?
Oh, yes; they were awfully pleased.
A rather nice-looking woman came down, in a big hat, and went into the garden with a young man, without saying a word.
That was Mother, I expect. We’re an independent family﻿—we entertain our friends sort of separately.
It was sweet of you to come.
I wanted to come﻿—I’ve thought about you a lot.
I mean it. You’re so alive and vital and different from other people.
I’m so frightened that you’ll be bored here.
Oh, I don’t know. But you won’t be, will you?﻿—or if you are, tell me at once, and we’ll do something quite different.
You’re rather a dear, you know.

I’m not﻿—I’m devastating, entirely lacking in restraint. So’s Simon. It’s Father’s and Mother’s fault really; you see, they’re so vague﻿—they’ve spent their lives cultivating their Arts and not devoting any time to ordinary conventions and manners and things. I’m the only one who sees that, so I’m trying to be better. I’d love to be beautifully poised and carry off difficult situations with a lift of the eyebrows﻿—
I’m sure you could carry off anything.
There you are, you see, saying the right thing! You always say the right thing, and no one knows a bit what you’re really thinking. That’s what I adore.
I’m afraid to say anything now, in case you think I’m only being correct.
But you are correct. I wish you’d teach Simon to be correct too.
It would be uphill work, I’m afraid.
I’ve only met him for a moment.
Would you like to see the garden?
As a matter of fact, we’d better wait until after tea. Shall I sing you something?

I don’t want to really a bit﻿—only I’m trying to entertain you. It’s as easy as pie to talk in someone else’s house, like at the dance the other night, but here on my own ground I’m finding it difficult.
Oh, it isn’t your fault; honestly, it isn’t﻿—you’re awfully kind and responsive. What shall we do?
Out in the garden, I think.
Oh, everyone will come dashing in, then. How awful!
Won’t the luggage get rather wet, out there?
I’ll bring it in when I’ve made the tea.
We ought to have got William up from the village.
Do sit down and smoke. I can easily manage it.
How typical of Myra to have so many bags.﻿ ﻿… Ooh!
He brings in a dressing-case, and wipes his hand on his handkerchief.
Do you know where to wash if you want to?
Reenter Clara, with tea and hot-water jug.
Simon and Myra come in from the garden.
Oh, yes; we’ve met several times.
Simon, come and be nice to Miss Coryton.
That’s no reason for you not to be nice to her.
You must forgive me for being rather frowsy, but I’ve been working hard.
How are you? When did you arrive?
He begins to pour it out.
She was last seen in the punt.
Oh, well, she’ll be all right then. Who is he?
There’s going to be a thunderstorm. I felt sick this morning. This is Sandy Tyrell﻿—everybody﻿—
Oh, yes. You were here before, weren’t you?
How far are you from Maidenhead exactly?
What a pity it’s raining﻿—we might have had some tennis﻿—
They both stop, to let the other go on. There is another terrible silence.
I adore the shape of this hall﻿—it’s so﻿—
The train was awfully crowded coming down﻿—
They both stop again, and there is another dead silence, during which the curtain slowly falls.
It is after dinner on the Saturday evening. Everyone is talking and arguing. The following scene should be played with great speed.
No; you always guess it too quickly.
What do we have to do?
Someone goes out, you see, and comes in, and you’ve chosen a word among yourselves, and she or he or whoever it is asks you some sort of question and you have to﻿—
Not an ordinary question, Simon; they have to ask them to do something in the manner of the word, and then﻿—
Then, you see, you act whatever it is﻿—
The answer to the question, you see?
Quite usual things, like reciting “If,” or playing the piano﻿—
Never mind; you can fake it, as long as it conveys an idea of the word.
The word we’ve all thought of?
I’m afraid I don’t quite understand yet.
Never mind; I’ll explain. You see, someone goes out.﻿ ﻿…
I’ll go out the first time, just to show her.
It’s quite simple﻿—all you have to do is just act in the manner of the word.
Look here, everybody, I’m going out.
The History game’s awfully good﻿—when two people go out, and come back as Queen Elizabeth and Crippen or somebody.
I’ll show you, Sandy. You see.﻿ ﻿…
There’s always “How, When and Where?” We haven’t played that for ages.
We will afterwards. We’ll do this one first.﻿—Go on, Sorel.
No, we did that last week; she’ll know.
There was an amusing game I played once at the Harringtons’ house. Everyone was blindfolded except﻿—
This room’s not big enough for that. What about “winsomely”?
I wish I knew what we had to do.
You’ll see when we start playing.
Mother’s brilliant at this. Do you remember when we played it at the Mackenzies’?
Yes, and Blanche was so cross when I kissed Freddie’s ear in the manner of the word.
She’s sure to guess it straight off.
Young Norman Robertson used to be marvellous﻿—do you remember?
He’s lost it all since his marriage.
I didn’t know you knew him.
Well, considering he married my cousin﻿—
We don’t seem to be getting on with the game.
We haven’t thought of a word yet.
“Saucily.” I’ve got a lovely idea for “saucily.”
The great thing is to get an obscure word.
What a pity Irene isn’t here﻿—she knows masses of obscure words.
She’s probably picked them up from her obscure friends.
It’s no use being catty about Irene; she’s a perfect darling.
I wasn’t being catty at all.
Yes, but we don’t happen to be doing them at the moment.
You haven’t got the right intonation a bit.
Oh, Mother darling, do shut up!
I don’t like “so long” very much.
Do you think we might go on now?
Go to the next one; I’m not going to do any more.
Oh, please do. You were simply splendid.
I believe you’ve muddled it up.
You’d better go on to the next one.
Which word were you doing? Whisper﻿—
Oh, I see. I’m so sorry.
No, it’s Jackie’s turn now; it will come round to him again, I’m afraid.
No, I’d much rather not. Count me out.
Really, the ridiculous fuss everyone makes﻿—
I’m awfully stupid at anything like this.
It’s only a game, after all.
Leave her alone if she doesn’t want to.
It’s awfully difficult if you haven’t done it before.
Go on to the next one.
Lose my temper! I like that! No one’s given me the slightest indication of what the word is﻿—you all argue and squabble﻿—
Talk, talk, talk! Everybody talks too much.
It’s so surprising to me when people won’t play up. After all﻿—
You haven’t played it at all yet.
Really, Simon, the way you go on is infuriating!
It’s always the way; whenever Sorel goes out she gets quarrelsome.
